passages.text: At dawn, when Peter came forward to converse, Simon spoke first: “As I left yesterday, I promised you that today I would return, debate with you, and show that the one who fashioned the world is not the highest God, but another, who alone is good and has remained unknown until now. To begin, then: do you say that the maker himself is also lawgiver, or not? If he is lawgiver, he is just; and being just, he is not good. If he is not good, Jesus proclaimed another when he said, ‘Do not call me good, for the good one is one, the Father in the heavens.’ This does not agree with the lawgiver’s being both just and good.” Peter said, “First tell us: on account of what actions does the good one seem to you good, and on account of what actions the just one just? In this way we can aim our arguments at the target.” Simon said, “You first tell us what seems to you good, and what just.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δίκαιος δὲ ὢν ἀγαθὸς οὐκ ἔστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: being just, he is not good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Simon’s opposition of justice and goodness as his claim, not the translator’s conclusion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: aim our arguments at the target
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the aiming/target image.

passages.text: Peter said, “So that I do not spend time in a more contentious debate, rightly demanding that you answer my questions, I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked. I say that the good person is the one who provides, as I see the maker himself doing when he provides the sun to good and evil people and rain to the righteous and unrighteous.” Simon said, “This is most unjust: he provides the same things to the righteous and unrighteous.” Peter said, “Then you tell us from now on how he would act to be good.” Simon said, “You must say.” Peter said, “I will. If, by providing the same things to the good and righteous and also to the evil and unrighteous, he is according to you not even just, and if, by providing good things to the good and bad things to the bad, you would reasonably call him just, what further course of action could he take, if not this way: providing temporary things to the evil, in case they change, and eternal things to the good, provided they remain? Thus, in providing for all but granting different gifts, his justice is good and all the more patient in this way: he forgives sinners their sins when they reorient and promises eternal life also to those who have acted well. But in judging at the end and assigning to each what is deserved, he is just. If, then, these matters rightly stand this way, acknowledge it; but if they do not seem right to you, refute them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who provides
lexical_decisions.rationale: Goodness is defined through giving/provision in this argument; generous is an alternative, but provision is kept explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he forgives sinners their sins when they reorient
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB moral-spiritual reorientation wording, traditionally repent, preserving forgiveness and its stated relation to the response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: promises eternal life
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπογράφω can pledge, prescribe, or outline. Promises fits the positive undertaking to those who act well, without claiming automatic possession already.

passages.text: Simon said, “I have said it once: every lawgiver, looking toward what is just, is just.” Peter said, “If it belongs to goodness not to lay down a law, and to justice to lay one down, even in this way the maker is both good and just: good because, from Adam’s time until Moses, he does not appear to have laid down the law in writing; and from Moses down to the present times, as it is written, he is also just.” Simon said, “Show from your teacher’s statements that it belongs to the same one to be good and just. For it seems impossible to me that the lawgiver, being good, is himself also just.” Peter said, “Listen to how the good itself is also just. Our teacher himself, when the Pharisee said, ‘What must I do to inherit eternal life?’ first said, ‘Do not call me good, for the good one is one, the Father in the heavens.’ Immediately afterward he added, ‘But if you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.’ When the man said, ‘Which ones?’ he directed him to those of the law. Had he been indicating someone else as good, he would not have referred him to the commandments of the just one. I myself also acknowledge that what is just is one thing and what is good another; but you do not know that being good and just belong to the same one. For he is good in being patient now with those who reorient and receiving them; and he is just when, in judging, he assigns to each what is deserved.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγγράφως οὐ φαίνεται τεθεικὼς τὸν νόμον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he does not appear to have laid down the law in writing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the in-writing qualification and appears, not an absolute claim that there was no divine instruction before Moses.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Pharisee
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s identification of the questioner rather than harmonizing it to a different designation in a familiar Gospel account.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who reorient
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology, traditionally those who repent, without an unprinted intensifier.

passages.text: Simon said, “How, then, when the maker was known—the one who formed Adam and was known to the righteous according to the law, and furthermore to the righteous and unrighteous and the whole world—does your teacher, coming after all those people, say, ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him’? He would not have said these things unless he were announcing a certain Father who is in secrecy, whom the law also calls Most High, from whom no good or evil utterance has been heard, as Jeremiah too testifies in the Lamentations. In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, who are seventy, and marking out the nations’ boundaries by seventy languages, this one gave the Hebrews as a portion to his Son, who is also called Lord and ordered heaven and earth, and appointed him God of gods. By gods I mean those who have received the other portions of the nations. Laws therefore issued from all the gods just mentioned to their own portions, namely the remaining nations; likewise the law established among the Hebrews issued from the Son, the Lord of all. It was determined to be this way so that if someone takes refuge in someone’s law, he becomes part of the portion of the one whose law he has undertaken to practice. No one knew the Most High Father who is in secrecy, just as no one knew of this one’s Son that he is Son. Indeed, you, assigning to the Son the distinctive attributes of the secret Most High, do not know that he is Son, being Father of the Jesus whom you call Messiah.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in secrecy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression can mean among unrevealed mysteries or in the secret realm. In secrecy preserves the hidden status without inventing a named location.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Israel, not another textual witness’s sons of God or angels; the explicit count seventy remains.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτοῦ υἱῷ τῷ καὶ „κυρίῳ“ λεγομένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to his Son, who is also called Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Simon’s distinction between the Most High and his Son, who is the maker in this proposal, not the translator’s own theological identification.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ καθ’ ὑμᾶς λεγομένου χριστοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Jesus whom you call Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστός is a disputed independent title attributed by Simon to the other party’s Jesus, so Messiah preserves the title’s force.

passages.text: After Simon said these things, Peter said to him, “Can you call that very one to witness that you believe this—not the one you now say is in secrecy, but the one you believe in without acknowledging him? For you talk nonsense by defining one thing in place of another. Therefore, if you call him to witness that you believe what you say, I will answer you; but if you stand debating with me things you do not believe, you force me to strike at emptiness.” Simon said, “I heard from one of your disciples ....” Peter said, “Do not bear false witness.” Simon said, “Do not abuse me, you utterly rash man.” Peter said, “Until you name the person who said it, you are a liar.” Simon said, “Suppose that I invented these things, or even heard them from someone else: answer me about them. For if they cannot be overturned, I have learned that this is the truth.” Peter said, “If it is a human fabrication, I will not answer it. But if you are held by its supposition as true, acknowledge this very thing to me, and I myself also have something to say about it.” Simon said, “Once for all, I think it is so. If you have anything to say about these things, answer.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: call ... to witness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The demand invokes the one actually believed in as witness, not a request for a merely informal reassurance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: strike at emptiness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the striking-at-a-void metaphor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . .
lexical_decisions.chosen: I heard from one of your disciples ....
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly four dots remain for the printed gap; the alleged disclosure’s missing content is not restored.

source_issues.source_quote: Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . .
source_issues.issue: Exactly four printed dots remain; the missing report is not reconstructed.

passages.text: Peter said, “If this is so, you act with the greatest impiety. For if it belongs to the Son who ordered heaven and earth to reveal his Father in secrecy to whomever he wishes, you, as I said, act with the greatest impiety by revealing to those to whom he did not reveal.” Simon said, “But he himself wants me to reveal.” Peter said, “You do not understand what I say, Simon. Yet listen and understand. Saying, ‘To those to whom the Son wishes he will reveal,’ does not mean that someone learns such a thing by teaching, but only by revelation. Revelation is what lies secretly in all human hearts, covered, being uncovered without a voice by his will. Thus one comes to know not by being taught, but by understanding. Yet the one who has understood is not permitted to demonstrate this to another, since he himself was not taught; nor can he reveal it, since he himself is not the Son—unless he says that he himself is the Son. But you are not the standing Son. For if you were Son, you would certainly know those worthy of such revelation. But you do not know. For if you knew, you would do the things done by those who know.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ φωνῆς τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλῆς ἀποκαλυπτόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: being uncovered without a voice by his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase can be grouped as without a voice, by his will, or without a voice expressing his will. The main rendering keeps the nonvocal disclosure and its relation to his will without adding spoken instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the standing Son
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the standing epithet and Son together, rather than replacing them with a later named title or deleting the unusual description.

passages.text: Simon said, “I admit I did not understand how you mean, ‘You would do the things done by those who know.’” Peter said, “If you did not understand, you also cannot know each person’s mind. And if you do not know, you also do not know those worthy of revelation. If you do not know, you are not Son; but the Son knows, and therefore reveals to those he wishes as being worthy.” Simon said, “Do not deceive: I know those who are worthy, and I am not Son. Yet I did not understand what this is, ‘He reveals to those he wishes,’ as you say. I said that I did not understand not because I did not know, but because I knew that those present did not understand, so that you would state it more clearly and those for whose sake we also conduct the discussion might understand.” Peter said, “I cannot state it more clearly. Since you have understood it, explain it yourself.” Simon said, “I am not obliged to state your views.” Peter said, “It seems to me, Simon, that you do not understand it and are unwilling to admit it, lest, being caught in ignorance, you be exposed as not being the standing Son. For this is what you hint at, even if you do not wish to say it plainly. Thus I know your intentions from your hints, being a disciple of a true prophet, not a prophet. But you, though you do not understand even what is plainly said, wish to call yourself Son, standing against us.” Simon said, “I will remove every excuse from you. I admit that I did not understand what this is: ‘And to those to whom the Son wishes, he reveals.’ So state it more clearly.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the standing Son
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the epithet tied to Simon’s alleged claim; it is not identified with an external historical person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προφήτου ἀληθοῦς μαθητὴς ὤν, οὐ προφήτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: being a disciple of a true prophet, not a prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Peter’s explicit denial of being a prophet in this statement, rather than harmonizing it to a later title.

passages.text: Peter said, “Since you have admitted, even if only for appearances, that you do not understand it, answer what I ask you, and you will learn. Tell me: do you say that the Son, whoever he may be, is just, or not?” Simon said, “Most just.” Peter said, “If he is just, why does he not reveal to all, but to those he wishes?” Simon said, “Because, being just, he wishes to reveal to those who are worthy.” Peter said, “Then must he not know each person’s mind so that he may reveal to the worthy?” Simon said, “It must certainly be so.” Peter said, “Then he alone was reasonably appointed to reveal, since he alone knows each person’s mind—not you, who cannot even understand the things we say.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: even if only for appearances
lexical_decisions.rationale: σχήματι can indicate outward form or pretense; even formally is a less interpretive alternative. The admission is treated skeptically, not accepted as sincere without qualification.

passages.text: After Peter said this, praise arose from the crowds. Simon, thoroughly exposed, blushed in shame, rubbed his forehead, and said, “But they call me a magician, defeated by Peter, and also caught in argument. Yet if someone is caught in argument and taken unawares, he does not thereby have the truth within him defeated; for the weakness of its defender is not the truth of the defeated party. Nevertheless I tell you that I judged everyone present worthy to know the Father in secrecy. Therefore, when I reveal him to them publicly, they should not be angry with me out of envy, since I wish to do them good.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: caught in argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: The form can mean reasoning or being brought under a syllogistic argument. The context of defeat and being taken unawares favors being caught in argument; reasoning is a material alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἡ ἀσθένεια τοῦ ἐκδικοῦντος ἀλήθειά ἐστιν τοῦ νικωμένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the weakness of its defender is not the truth of the defeated party
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the compact distinction between a weak defender and the truth he defends rather than rewriting it as truth’s weakness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ αὐτοῖς διὰ φθόνον ἐμοὶ τῷ εὐεργετεῖν αὐτοὺς θέλοντι χαλεπαίνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they should not be angry with me out of envy, since I wish to do them good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes αὐτοῖς as the persons for whom getting angry is inappropriate, leaving the grammatical third-person reference intact instead of silently changing it to you, Peter.

passages.text: Peter said, “Since you have spoken in this way to please the crowds present, I will speak not to please them, but truthfully. Tell me: how do you know that everyone present is worthy, when not even one agreed with you as you disclosed it? For their praising me against you is not the act of people agreeing with you, but with me, to whom they also assigned praise as someone who had spoken rightly. But since God, being just, judges each person’s mind—which you say is true—he would not have wished this to be given to those on the right through the left. By the same reasoning, someone who receives anything from a thief is himself liable. Therefore, for this reason, he did not wish them to receive what you bring, but rather through the Son appointed to reveal. For to whom is it reasonable to reveal the Father, except the Son alone, because he knows the person worthy of such revelation? Thus this cannot be taught or learned by teaching, but must be revealed by an inexpressible hand to the one worthy to know it.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to those on the right through the left
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the right/left opposition without identifying unprinted named camps or persons.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by an inexpressible hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the hand image, not merely a generic divine act.

passages.text: Simon said, “For a combatant, using his own weapons contributes greatly to victory. For what someone loves he can also genuinely defend, and what is genuinely defended possesses no ordinary strength. Therefore from now on I will set out what I really think. I say that there is a certain power in secrecy, unknown to everyone, even to the maker himself—as Jesus himself also said, without knowing what he uttered; for sometimes, through much talking, someone hits upon the truth without knowing what he says. I am also speaking about this statement he made: ‘No one knew the Father.’” Peter said, “No longer claim to know his teachings.” Simon said, “I do not claim to believe his teachings; I am debating with you about the things he happened to get right.” Peter said, “So as not to give you an excuse to flee, I will discuss with you as you wish. Nevertheless I call everyone to witness that you do not believe even the argument you have now stated. For I know what you think. And so that you do not think I am lying, I will hint at your own views, so that you may see you are conversing with someone who knows.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what someone loves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object can be a position or cause, not necessarily a person; this introduces the own-weapons metaphor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things he happened to get right
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Simon’s disparaging account of accidental truth rather than endorsing his claim as a narrator’s assessment.

passages.text: “We, Simon, do not say that two angels were sent from the great power, also called the sovereign power, one to create a world and the other to lay down the law. Nor do we say that each came to the things he had made and announced himself as their original author. Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary. Learn how you disbelieve even this hypothesis. The power you say is in secrecy is full of ignorance, for it did not foreknow the ingratitude of the angels it sent.” While Peter was saying this, Simon became very angry and interrupted him, saying, “Why do you babble, you bold and utterly rash man, plainly disclosing the secrets before uninstructed crowds?” Peter said, “Why do you begrudge the benefit given to the hearers present?” Simon said, “Then do you acknowledge that such knowledge is a benefit?” Peter said, “I do: for once falsehood is known, it gives the benefit of not falling into it through ignorance.” Simon said, “It seems to me that you cannot answer what I put before you. I mean that your teacher too says that there is a certain Father in secrecy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς μεγάλης δυνάμεως, ἔτι τε καὶ τῆς κυρίας λεγομένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: the great power, also called the sovereign power
lexical_decisions.rationale: κυρίας can qualify power as sovereign, ruling, or mistress-like; sovereign power gives its authority sense without adding a separate named deity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominal clause is extremely compressed. The main rendering carries do we speak from the preceding repeated denial and preserves standing, future standing, and adversary without supplying a named identity. Nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary is another possible grouping.

lexical_decisions.chosen: plainly disclosing the secrets
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀτέχνως here means plainly or without qualification, not necessarily in an unskilled manner.

source_issues.issue: The nominal clause leaves its finite verbal relation implicit. The main text carries the preceding denial of doctrinal assertion forward; a direct nominal assertion, nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary, is another grouping. Every surviving element remains.

passages.text: Peter said, “I will answer what you want, concerning ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.’ First, I am amazed how, when this statement has countless interpretations, you chose the more dangerous part, saying that the statement referred to ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him. For in the first place the statement can have been addressed to all the Jews who supposed David to be the Messiah’s father and did not recognize the Messiah himself as Son and as Son of God. Therefore it was appropriately said, ‘No one knew the Father,’ since everyone named David instead of God. He added, ‘Nor does anyone know the Son,’ because they did not know that he was Son. Saying, ‘Those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him,’ was also rightly said, for the Son who has existed from the beginning alone was appointed to reveal to those he wishes. Thus it is possible for Adam, the first formed, not to have been ignorant of him; for Enoch, who pleased him, not to have been without knowledge; for righteous Noah not to have been without understanding; for Abraham the friend not to have failed to comprehend; nor for Isaac not to have understood, nor for Jacob who wrestled not to have believed, nor for him to have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you chose the more dangerous part
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the comparative, not the unsupported superlative most dangerous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἀγνωσίαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πάντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitives are taken as subjective: maker and created ones are ignorant of the secret Father, as in Simon’s argument. Ignorance of the maker is an objective-genitive alternative, but fits the immediately preceding exchange less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor for him to have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final coordinated clause is taken within the negative scope carried by the preceding οὐχ ... μὴ and οὐχ ... μὴ clauses. The overt μὴ is represented by unrevealed; nor carries the shared denial. A clause-local reading would instead say and not to have been revealed, which breaks the preceding parallel argument. This grouping is disclosed rather than silently dropping the negative.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
source_issues.issue: The final clause has μὴ but no newly repeated οὐχ. The rendering carries the preceding negative scope across the coordination, yielding nor ... unrevealed. Reading the final clause independently would yield and not revealed, an alternative at odds with the preceding parallel argument.

passages.text: But if, as you say, it is now through Jesus that he is revealed to everyone for knowledge, how do you not call it most unjust that those men did not know him—seven pillars of the world who were able to please the most just God—while now so many from the nations, impious in every way, know him? Were those men not deemed worthy to know the one better than all? And how is what is not just good? Unless by good you wish to mean not the one who benefits those who have acted justly, but the one who loves the unrighteous even if they do not believe, revealing to them also the secrets that he was unwilling to reveal to the righteous. Such conduct belongs neither to a good nor to a just being, but to one who hates the reverent. Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon, who is so emboldened as to say that these things were spoken in a way they never were?

lexical_decisions.chosen: seven pillars of the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the stated seven without supplying an unprinted list of names.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήτι σὺ εἶ, Σίμων, ὁ ἑστώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the standing epithet and interrogative challenge, not a translator’s identification of Simon.

passages.text: Indignant at this, Simon said, “I accuse your teacher, who said, ‘I give thanks to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because the things that were hidden from the wise you revealed to nursing infants.’” Peter said, “The statement was not spoken in this way. But first I will speak as though it had been said as you supposed. Even if our Lord had said, ‘The things that were hidden from the wise, these the Father revealed to infants,’ he would not even in this way be thought to indicate a God and Father other than the one who created the world. For the hidden things he spoke of can belong to the maker himself, since Isaiah also said, ‘I will open my mouth in parables and pour out things hidden from the foundation of the world.’ Do you therefore acknowledge the prophet who was not ignorant of the hidden things that Jesus says were concealed from the wise but revealed to infants? How was the maker ignorant when his prophet Isaiah was not ignorant? But our Jesus in fact did not say, ‘The things that were hidden,’ but spoke what seems harsher; for he said, ‘You revealed them to nursing infants.’ As for saying, ‘You hid’—. For the key of the kingdom of the heavens lay with them, that is, knowledge of the secrets.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since Isaiah also said
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains this author’s attribution to Isaiah; it is not corrected from a different canonical text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the secrets
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes unrevealed matters or mysteries, not a specified later system of esoteric doctrine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ εἰπεῖν „ἀπέκρυψας“, ὡς ποτε ἔγνω σμέων αὐτοῖς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: As for saying, ‘You hid’—.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final construction after you hid is not translated because the supplied separated ἔγνω σμέων does not yield a defensible contextual reading. No dots are invented to pretend this is a printed lacuna; the omission is explicitly blocking in source_issues pending inspection, not accepted coverage.

source_issues.issue: Genuine unresolved construction: the separated ἔγνω σμέων cannot currently be given a defensible contextual English rendering. This phrase is omitted rather than conjecturally repaired, so coverage is incomplete and publication is blocked. The construction needs comparison with the printed source. This is not a printed lacuna, and no artificial dot gap has been supplied.

passages.text: And do not say, “He acted impiously toward the wise by hiding these things from them.” Far be it from us to suppose this. For he did not act impiously. Rather, because they hid the knowledge of the kingdom and neither entered themselves nor allowed those who wished to enter, for this reason, in accordance with justice, just as they themselves hid the ways from those who wished, so the secrets were also hidden from them. This was so that what they had done might happen likewise to them, and with the measure they measured, it might be measured to them equally. For the worthy person is owed knowledge of what he does not know; but from the unworthy person it is taken away, even if he seems to possess it and is wise in other matters, and given to the worthy, even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τῆς μαθητείας ὦσιν νήπιοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Infants here is explicitly qualified by time in discipleship, not necessarily literal nursing children. The metaphor is retained rather than silently harmonizing all infant-language.

passages.text: If someone says, “Nothing was hidden from the sons of Israel, because it is written, ‘Nothing escaped you, Israel; for do not say, Jacob, “The way was hidden from me,”’” one must understand that the matters important to the kingdom were hidden from them, but the way leading into the kingdom, which is a manner of life, was not hidden. This is why he also says, “For do not say that the way was hidden from me.” The way is the manner of life, since Moses too says, “Look, I have set before your face the way of life and the way of death.” In agreement the teacher said, “Enter through the narrow and constricted way, through which you will enter life.” Elsewhere, when someone asked, “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” he pointed out the law’s commandments.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which is a manner of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here is conduct or way of living, not a political constitution.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τῆς στενῆς καὶ τεθλιμμένης ὁδοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: through the narrow and constricted way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains way as quoted here, not an imported gate from another witness.

passages.text: From Isaiah’s saying in God’s person, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” it does not follow that Isaiah too was hinting at a God other than the known maker. Rather, through a different riddle he called the known one unknown, because the people, ignorant of the known God’s just disposition, sinned and did not suppose that they would be judged by the good God. Therefore, after saying, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” he added, “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins.” For, as I said, through ignorance of his justice they were without fear and became full of sins, supposing him only good, in the sense that he would not pursue their sins.

lexical_decisions.chosen: just disposition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the disposition/character sense; the argument concerns ignorance of justice, not ignorance that any deity exists.

lexical_decisions.chosen: only good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the restrictive only, which is central to the polemic against separating goodness from judgment.

passages.text: Some sinned in this way from the supposition that, because of his goodness, he does not judge; others from the opposite view. For, supposing the statements of the scriptures against God to be true, although they are unjust and false, they did not know his true divinity and power. Therefore, supposing that he is ignorant, delights in murders, lets the wicked off through gifts of sacrifices, and also deceives, lies, and does everything unjust, they themselves, doing things like God, insisted while sinning that they were acting reverently. Therefore they were immovable toward what is better, and when admonished did not turn back. For they had no fear, considering themselves made like God through such actions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς γὰρ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν γραφῶν φωνάς, ἀδίκους οὔσας καὶ ψευδεῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the statements of the scriptures against God ... although they are unjust and false
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the historical speaker’s explicit criticism of certain scriptural statements. It is neither softened nor presented as the translator’s own verdict about scripture.

lexical_decisions.chosen: did not turn back
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

passages.text: One might reasonably say that the words, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father,” were addressed to those who supposed him to be like this. And rightly so. For had they known, they would not have sinned by believing books really written against God for testing. Elsewhere too, wishing to show them more clearly the cause of their error, he says, “This is why you are deceived: you do not know the true things in the scriptures, and for this reason you are also ignorant of God’s power.” Therefore every person who wants to be saved must become, as the teacher said, a judge of the books written for testing. For he said this: “Become approved money changers.” Money changers are needed because the counterfeit is also mixed in with the genuine.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the true things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinction within the scriptures asserted by the author; it is not replaced by simply the scriptures.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: πειρασμός can mean testing or temptation. The argument treats problematic books as a test of discernment; the temptation alternative remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Become approved money changers
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the money-changing analogy and the approved/genuine versus counterfeit contrast.

passages.text: After Peter said these things, Simon pretended to be shocked at what had been said about the scriptures and, as though alarmed, said, “Far be it from me and those who love me to listen to your statements. Until I knew that you held these views about the scriptures, I put up with you and conversed; but now I withdraw. I ought, however, to have withdrawn at the beginning, because I heard you say, ‘I believe no one who says anything against the one who created the world: neither angels nor prophets, neither scriptures nor priests, neither teachers nor anyone else, even if someone performs signs and wonders, even if he visibly flashes in the air or reveals through visions or dreams.’ Who, then, can persuade you, whether rightly or wrongly, to think anything other than what you have decided, when you remain so firmly and immovably in your own knowledge?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: pretended to be shocked
lexical_decisions.rationale: The narrator explicitly presents the shock as pretense, rather than leaving its sincerity open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: visibly flashes in the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the vivid flashing and airborne manifestation, not a generic vision.

passages.text: As Simon said this and was about to go out, Peter said, “Hear this further thing from me, then go wherever you wish.” Simon turned and remained, and Peter said, “I know how you were astounded then when you heard me say, ‘Whoever says anything against the God who created the world, I do not believe him.’ Now hear something greater than this. If the God who created the world really were in character such as the scriptures describe him, and even if in some other way he were incomparably evil, beyond what either the scriptures could say or anyone else could even conceive, I would nevertheless not stop revering him alone and doing his will. For I want you to know and be persuaded that the person who has no affection for his own maker can never have it for another either. If he does have it for another, he has it contrary to nature and does not know that he has from the evil one the love of the unjust, since he cannot even keep that love firm. And if there really is someone else above the maker, being good he will receive me all the more because I love my own Father; but he will not receive you, knowing that you abandoned your maker by nature—I do not say father—for a greater hope, without concern for what is reasonable. Thus, if you find someone stronger even than him, he knows that you will abandon him too someday, especially since he has not become your father, when you have abandoned even your true father.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν τῷ ὄντι ὁ τὸν κόσμον κτίσας θεὸς τὴν γνώμην τοιοῦτος ὢν τυγχάνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: If the God who created the world really were in character such as ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: The description is explicitly hypothetical. The severe conditional is preserved, not rewritten as an assertion that the maker is evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ πονηροῦ τὸν τῶν ἀδίκων ἔρωτα ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: he has from the evil one the love of the unjust
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive can mean love characteristic of unjust people or love directed toward the unjust. The main text retains the ambiguity of love of the unjust; from evil is also possible for ἐκ πονηροῦ rather than the personal evil one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν φύσει σου ποιητὴν (οὐ γὰρ λέγω πατέρα)
lexical_decisions.chosen: your maker by nature—I do not say father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Peter’s pointed change from father to maker in addressing Simon rather than harmonizing all parent-language.

passages.text: But you will say, “He knows that no one else is above him, and for this reason he cannot be abandoned.” Then thanks are due to there being no other! Yet he knows the disposition of your mind to be ready for ingratitude. If, knowing you to be ungrateful, he receives you, but knowing me to be grateful does not admit me, according to your account he is irrational, not acting reasonably. Thus, Simon, you are a subordinate of evil without knowing it.” Simon replied, “Then tell us: from where has evil grown?” Peter said, “Since today you already moved to go out and said that from now on you would not listen to me as a blasphemer, if you wish to learn, come tomorrow and I will explain. I will also allow you to examine me as you wish, without contentiousness.” Simon said, “I will do as seems good to me.” After saying this, he went away. None of those who had entered with him went out with him; instead, falling at Peter’s feet, they asked to obtain forgiveness for having been attached to Simon and to be received as they reoriented. Peter welcomed both those feeling regret and the other crowds, laid his hands on them, praying and healing the afflicted among them. Thus, as he dismissed them, he instructed them to hurry at dawn. After saying this, he went inside with his companions and did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them, since evening had arrived.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Then thanks are due to there being no other
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the ironic thanks and the existential absence, not a moral endorsement of Simon’s fidelity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to be received as they reoriented
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology for the moral-spiritual response, traditionally repenting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those feeling regret
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps μεταμέλομαι’s regret/remorse sense distinct from the preceding μετανοέω, rather than homogenizing both as reorienting.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ εἰωθότα πρὸς τὴν ἐπείγουσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐποίησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The customary practices are not enumerated here; neither a meal nor a particular prayer is invented.
